passages.happening:
After tearing themselves away from the Ephesian elders, Paul and his companions sail to Cos, then Rhodes, then Patara (verse 1). There they find a ship crossing to Phoenicia and board it (verse 2). They sight Cyprus, pass south of it, and land at Tyre in Syria, where the ship is to unload its cargo (verse 3).

They look up the disciples in Tyre and stay seven days. “Through the Spirit they kept telling Paul not to go up to Jerusalem” (verse 4). When the time comes to leave, all the disciples, with their wives and children, walk with them out of the city, and they kneel down on the beach to pray (verse 5). After saying goodbye, Paul's group goes aboard, and the others return home (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The ‘we’ continues: the writer is on the ship. Cos and Rhodes are islands off the south-west coast of what is now Turkey; Patara was a port on the mainland. From there a larger ship takes them straight across the open sea toward Phoenicia, the coast of what is now Lebanon.

Tyre was an old port city. There was already a church there, probably begun by believers scattered after Stephen's death (11:19). Paul did not plant it, but he finds brothers and sisters waiting.

And they say something hard. ‘Through the Spirit they kept telling Paul not to go up to Jerusalem.’ Paul has already said that the Spirit is leading him to Jerusalem and warning him of chains there (20:22-23). How can the Spirit say both? The note on verses 7-14 below takes up the question.

Then a lovely picture: whole families, wives and children, walking with the travellers out of the city and kneeling on the sand to pray. The church in Tyre had known Paul only a week.
passages.ot:
Tyre had a long history in the Old Testament. Its king Hiram sent cedar and craftsmen for Solomon's temple (1 Kings 5:1-10), and the prophets spoke against its pride (Ezekiel 27 and 28). Now there are believers in Tyre, praying on its beach with a Jewish apostle.

Prayer at a parting runs through Scripture. When Solomon dedicated the temple, he prayed kneeling before the altar of the LORD, with his hands spread out toward heaven (1 Kings 8:54).
passages.asks: A church that had known Paul for a week walked him to the shore and knelt in the sand to pray. Ask how you treat Christians passing through your life: visitors, newcomers, people who will soon move on. And ask whether you pray with the people you love when you part from them.

passages.t: Philip's daughters, and Agabus with the belt
passages.happening:
From Tyre they sail to Ptolemais, greet the believers there and stay a day (verse 7). The next day they go on to Caesarea and stay at the home of Philip the evangelist, one of the Seven (verse 8). “He had four unmarried daughters who prophesied” (verse 9).

After several days a prophet named Agabus comes down from Judea (verse 10). He takes Paul's belt, ties up his own feet and hands, and says, “The Holy Spirit says: ‘In this way the Jews of Jerusalem will bind the owner of this belt and hand him over to the Gentiles’” (verse 11).

When they hear this, Paul's companions and the local believers beg him not to go up to Jerusalem (verse 12). Paul answers, “Why are you weeping and breaking my heart? I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus” (verse 13). When he will not be persuaded, they fall silent and say, “The Lord’s will be done” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Philip was one of the seven men chosen in chapter 6 to care for widows (6:5). He preached in Samaria and baptized the Ethiopian official, and then came to Caesarea (8:40). That was many years earlier. He has been living there since, and he is called ‘the evangelist’, one who tells the good news.

He has four unmarried daughters ‘who prophesied’. Luke states it plainly. These young women spoke God's word to the church. At Pentecost Peter quoted Joel: ‘Your sons and daughters will prophesy’ (2:17). Here are daughters doing so. Christians agree that women prophesied in the early church; Paul speaks of women who pray and prophesy (1 Corinthians 11:5). They differ on what that means for women's roles in the church today, much as they do over Priscilla teaching Apollos; the note on Acts 18:24-28 sets out the complementarian and egalitarian readings, and these notes do not choose between them.

Agabus is the same prophet who foretold the famine (11:28). Now he acts out his message, as the Old Testament prophets often did. He ties his own hands and feet with Paul's belt, and says this is what will happen to its owner.

‘The Jews of Jerusalem will bind’ him. Agabus is a Jewish believer speaking of what some in Jerusalem will do, and the events that follow show it was a crowd stirred up by some Jews from Asia (verse 27). It is not a word against the Jewish people; the note on Acts 13:42-47 sets out how this site reads such phrases. And notice the second half: they will hand him over ‘to the Gentiles’, the Romans. As with Jesus, Jews and Gentiles are both part of the story.

Everyone weeps. Even the writer, the ‘we’ of the story, begs Paul not to go. Paul is moved, ‘breaking my heart’, but not turned. In the end the friends say, ‘The Lord's will be done.’
passages.ot:
Acted-out prophecy was the way of Israel's prophets. Jeremiah was told, “Go and buy yourself a linen loincloth and put it around your waist” (Jeremiah 13:1), as a sign of Judah's pride. Ezekiel drew Jerusalem on a brick and lay beside it (Ezekiel 4:1-8). Isaiah went barefoot for three years “as a sign and omen against Egypt and Cush” (Isaiah 20:3).

Women prophets are part of Israel's story: “Miriam the prophetess” (Exodus 15:20), Deborah (Judges 4:4) and Huldah (2 Kings 22:14). And Joel had promised, “Your sons and daughters will prophesy” (Joel 2:28).
passages.hard:
Was Paul right to go? The believers at Tyre spoke ‘through the Spirit’ telling him not to go (verse 4), and his friends in Caesarea begged him to stay. Yet Paul said he was going ‘compelled by the Spirit’ (20:22). Readers differ.

Most readers think the Spirit showed the believers what was coming, chains and suffering, and that out of love they concluded Paul should not go. The warning was the Spirit's; the advice was their own. Agabus himself only foretells; he does not forbid. Paul accepted the warning but not the advice, because he believed the Spirit was calling him into that suffering, as Jesus had set his face toward Jerusalem (Luke 9:51). Later, in Jerusalem, the risen Lord stands by Paul and tells him he must testify in Rome too (23:11), which many read as God's approval of the road he took.

A few readers think Paul was mistaken: that he should have listened, and that the trouble that followed shows it. Luke's own telling leans toward Paul, but he lets the tension stand.

One thing is clear from the story: guidance is not a formula. Good people who loved Paul and prayed sincerely reached a different conclusion from him. Hearing God involves Scripture, prayer, the counsel of others, and sometimes a hard decision that friends do not share. ‘The Lord's will be done’ was the way they kept peace with one another when they could not agree.
passages.asks: Paul's friends wept and begged him to stay, and he went anyway, and they ended by saying, ‘The Lord's will be done.’ Ask how you respond when someone you love makes a costly choice for God that you would not make. And ask what you would be willing to suffer for the name of Jesus.

passages.t: James and the elders, and a vow in the temple
passages.happening:
After this they go up to Jerusalem, staying with Mnason, a believer from Cyprus (verses 15-16). The believers welcome them gladly (verse 17). The next day Paul goes to see James, with all the elders present (verse 18), and tells them, one thing after another, what God has done among the Gentiles (verse 19).

They praise God. Then they say: “You see, brother, how many thousands of Jews have believed, and all of them are zealous for the law” (verse 20). But they have heard that Paul teaches all the Jews living among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, “telling them not to circumcise their children or observe our customs” (verse 21).

So the elders advise him: four men among them have taken a vow. Paul should join them, purify himself with them, and pay their expenses so they can have their heads shaved. Then everyone will know the rumours are false and that Paul himself keeps the law (verses 23-24). As for the Gentile believers, the elders repeat the letter they sent them (verse 25). The next day Paul does as they ask and goes into the temple to give notice of when the offerings will be made (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
This James is the brother of Jesus, the leader of the Jerusalem church (15:13). Paul has probably brought the gift from the Gentile churches (24:17).

‘Many thousands of Jews have believed, and all of them are zealous for the law.’ The Jerusalem church was full of Jewish believers in Jesus who kept the law of Moses gladly: circumcising their sons, keeping the Sabbath, the feasts and the food laws, worshipping at the temple. The leaders see no conflict between trusting Jesus as Messiah and keeping the law as Jews. Nothing in the text treats their zeal as a fault. It was the faithfulness of Jews who had found their Messiah.

The rumour about Paul was that he told Jews living among Gentiles to stop circumcising their sons and to give up the customs. That was not what he taught. He fought against requiring circumcision of Gentiles, and against anyone treating the law as the way to be made right with God. But he had written, “Was a man already circumcised when he was called? He should not become uncircumcised” (1 Corinthians 7:18).

So the elders suggest a public act. Four men have taken a vow, most likely a Nazirite vow, which ended with shaving the head and offering sacrifices at the temple. The offerings were costly, and paying them for poorer men was seen as an act of devotion. Paul will pay, and will go through the rite of purification with them. Luke does not say exactly why Paul himself needed purifying; many think it was because he had come from long travels among Gentiles.

Verse 25 repeats the letter of chapter 15 for Gentile believers. The Jerusalem leaders keep both decisions: Gentiles are not asked to keep the whole law, and Jews are not asked to give it up.
passages.ot:
The vow was the Nazirite vow of the Law. At its end, the Nazirite was to present “an unblemished year-old male lamb as a burnt offering, an unblemished year-old female lamb as a sin offering” (Numbers 6:14), with other offerings, and shave his head at the entrance to the sanctuary (Numbers 6:18). A Nazirite made unclean during the vow had to shave his head “on the day of his cleansing” (Numbers 6:9), which was the seventh day.

The love of the law that marked these believers is the love of the Psalms: “Oh, how I love Your law! All day long it is my meditation” (Psalm 119:97).
passages.hard:
How does Paul joining a temple vow fit with his letter to the Galatians, where he says “by works of the law no one will be justified” (Galatians 2:16) and warns that anyone who gets himself circumcised “is obligated to obey the whole law” (Galatians 5:3)? Readers answer in different ways, and these notes do not settle the question.

Many see no contradiction. Paul fought against the law being made a condition of salvation, or forced on Gentiles. But he never said that Jews who believed in Jesus must stop living as Jews. He kept Jewish ways when he chose to, as with his own vow at Cenchrea (18:18), and he wrote, “To the Jews I became like a Jew, to win the Jews” (1 Corinthians 9:20). He also wrote, “Do we, then, nullify the law by this faith? Certainly not! Instead, we uphold the law” (Romans 3:31). On this view, paying for the vow was an act of love for his people and of peace with Jewish believers, not a step back from the gospel.

Some scholars think Luke has shown Paul as more law-keeping than the Paul of the letters would have been, to stress the unity of the church. Others think Paul did join the vow, but that it was a compromise under pressure, and point out that it did not work: the riot began in the temple a few days later. The book page's part ‘Acts and Paul's letters’ sets these tensions out.

On any view, the scene shows the first church holding two kinds of believers together at real cost: Jewish believers zealous for the law, and Gentile believers free from it, joined in one faith in one Lord.
passages.asks: James and the elders rejoiced at God's work among the Gentiles and cared deeply for the Jewish believers who kept the law. Ask whether you can rejoice at God's work among people whose worship looks very different from yours. And notice what Paul did with a false rumour about himself: not a long defence, but an act of humility. Ask how you answer false things said about you.

passages.happening:
When the seven days are almost over, some Jews from the province of Asia see Paul in the temple. They stir up the whole crowd and seize him (verse 27), shouting, “Men of Israel, help us! This is the man who teaches everywhere against our people and against our law and against this place” (verse 28). They add that he has brought Greeks into the temple and defiled this holy place. They had earlier seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and assumed Paul had brought him into the temple (verse 29).

The whole city is stirred up. People run together, seize Paul, drag him out of the temple, and at once the gates are shut (verse 30). While they are trying to kill him, word reaches the commander of the Roman regiment that all Jerusalem is in turmoil (verse 31). He takes soldiers and centurions and runs down to the crowd, and when the people see them, they stop beating Paul (verse 32).

The commander arrests Paul, orders him bound with two chains, and asks who he is and what he has done (verse 33). The crowd shouts one thing and another, so he orders Paul taken into the barracks (verse 34). On the steps the soldiers have to carry him because of the violence of the mob (verse 35), for the crowd keeps shouting, “Away with him!” (verse 36).
passages.hearers:
Who started this? Luke says plainly: ‘some Jews from the province of Asia’, pilgrims in Jerusalem for the feast who knew Paul from Ephesus. Not the Jewish people, and not the thousands of Jewish believers in the city. A group of opponents stirred up a crowd with a false charge. Paul, a Jew who had just paid for a vow in the temple, is the one attacked. The note on Acts 2:22-28 explains how verses like this were later turned against the Jewish people, and why this site rejects that reading.

The charge was serious. The temple had a low barrier that marked how far a non-Jew could go. Stone notices set along it, in Greek and in Latin, warned foreigners not to pass, on pain of death. The Jewish historian Josephus describes them. In 1871 one was found complete, its Greek wording very close to what Josephus says, and a broken second copy came to light in 1936. Historians still argue over whether anyone was ever actually put to death under it.

Trophimus was a Gentile believer from Ephesus, one of the men carrying the gift (20:4). Some had seen him in the city with Paul, and ‘assumed’ Paul had taken him past the barrier. He had not. A guess became a rumour, the rumour became a riot, and a man nearly died.

The temple gates are shut, probably to keep the holy place from being stained with blood. Then the Romans arrive. A Roman fortress, the Antonia, stood at the north-west corner of the temple area, with stairs leading down into the courts, so soldiers could reach the crowd quickly at feast times. The ‘commander’ led the soldiers stationed there; in Greek his title means ‘commander of a thousand’. Later we learn his name, Claudius Lysias (23:26).

The Romans do not rescue Paul out of kindness. They arrest him to stop a riot. He is bound with two chains, exactly as Agabus had acted out. And the crowd's cry, ‘Away with him’, is the cry that was raised against Jesus (Luke 23:18).
passages.ot:
The temple's boundary had its roots in the Law and the Prophets, which kept the sanctuary holy: “No foreigner uncircumcised in heart and flesh may enter My sanctuary” (Ezekiel 44:9). Yet Isaiah had also seen a day when foreigners who love the LORD would come to his house, “for My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations” (Isaiah 56:7).

A prophet seized in the temple by a crowd is an old story. When Jeremiah spoke in the LORD's house, “the priests and prophets and all the people seized him” (Jeremiah 26:8).
passages.asks: A guess about Trophimus became a riot that almost killed a man. Ask how quickly you believe and repeat what you have assumed about someone. And notice that Paul was attacked in the very act of honouring the temple and his people. Ask whether you are ready to be misunderstood even when you are doing right.

passages.happening:
As they are about to take Paul into the barracks, he asks the commander, “May I say something to you?” “Do you speak Greek?” the commander replies (verse 37). “Aren’t you the Egyptian who incited a rebellion some time ago and led four thousand members of the ‘Assassins’ into the wilderness?” (verse 38).

Paul answers, “I am a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no ordinary city. Now I beg you to allow me to speak to the people” (verse 39). With permission, Paul stands on the steps and motions to the crowd. A great hush falls, and he speaks to them in Hebrew (verse 40).
passages.hearers:
The commander is surprised that his prisoner speaks educated Greek. He had guessed Paul was a known rebel.

‘The Egyptian’ was a real man. The Jewish historian Josephus tells of an Egyptian who claimed to be a prophet, in the years when Felix was governor. He gathered followers and led them to the Mount of Olives, facing the city, promising that at his command Jerusalem's walls would fall. Roman troops attacked, many of his followers were killed or captured, and the Egyptian himself escaped. Josephus tells the story twice and gives different numbers: in one account about thirty thousand followers, in the other four hundred killed and two hundred captured. Luke's ‘four thousand’ is another figure. Ancient numbers like these were often rough.

‘The Assassins’ translates a Latin word, sicarii, ‘dagger-men’. Josephus describes them too: men who hid short daggers under their clothes and killed their opponents in the crowds at the feasts. Jerusalem in these years was tense and violent, and the commander thought he had caught a dangerous man.

Paul answers calmly. He is a Jew, from Tarsus, a proud and well-known city in Cilicia. He is not a rebel. And he asks to speak to the very crowd that has just beaten him.

He speaks ‘in Hebrew’. That may mean the Hebrew language itself, or Aramaic, the everyday language of Jews in Judea; scholars differ. Either way, he speaks in the language of his people, and they fall silent to listen. What he says comes in the next chapter.
passages.ot:
The Mount of Olives, where the Egyptian gathered his followers, had a place in Israel's hope. Zechariah foresaw the day when the LORD's “feet will stand on the Mount of Olives” (Zechariah 14:4). The Egyptian promised a sign like the fall of Jericho's walls (Joshua 6:20). He brought death instead.

Paul's calm before an angry crowd fits the wisdom of Proverbs: “A gentle answer turns away wrath” (Proverbs 15:1).
passages.asks: Beaten, chained and mistaken for a terrorist, Paul asked to speak to the crowd that had just tried to kill him. Ask whether you would want to speak to people who had hurt you, and what you would say. And notice the hush. Even an angry crowd can listen when someone speaks to them in their own language, as one of them.
